items.title: 2.10 Applying Predicate Logic to Real-World Problems

source_refs.note: Topic 2.10 with the Do You Know box, the headings Representing Relationships Using Predicates, Writing Logical Statements With Quantifiers and Reasoning and drawing conclusions, and the Class Activity, as printed (PDF 32-33, printed 28-29).

blocks.text: Predicate logic can be used to solve real-world problems by representing knowledge clearly and systematically. It helps us model situations involving objects, their properties, and relationships. Using predicate logic, we can analyze problems, make decisions, and find solutions logically.

blocks.title: Do You Know?
blocks.text: Predicate logic can model family trees, social networks, and even computer programs!

Predicates can represent relationships between objects in the real world. For example, Borrows(x, y) means “student x borrows book y,” and Teaches(t, s) means “teacher t teaches student s.” These predicates clearly describe how students, books, and teachers are connected. Using such relationships, we can model the working of the library system. This makes it easier to organize and understand interactions between different entities.

Quantifiers help us write general rules about the library. For example, ∀x, Student(x) → Borrows(x, Book) means “every student borrows a book.” ∃y, Book(y) ∧ Available(y) means “there exists at least one book that is available.” These statements help define rules and conditions in a precise way. Quantifiers allow us to describe both general situations and specific cases in the library system.

blocks.title: Class Activity
blocks.text: Ask students to write rules like “All students must attend class” using universal quantifiers.
Using predicate logic, we can draw conclusions from given facts. For example, if “∀x, Student(x) → HasLibraryCard(x)” and “Ali is a student,” then we conclude “Ali has a library card.”
This logical reasoning helps in decision making, such as checking whether a student can borrow a book. It ensures correct and consistent conclusions, making the system reliable and easy to manage.
